name: Greenspun's Tenth Rule
statement: Any big enough C or Fortran program contains a bad reimplementation of half of Lisp.
statementAccent: a bad reimplementation of half of Lisp
meaning: Large programs written in low-level languages tend to reinvent — badly — the high-level features Lisp provides natively: garbage collection, dynamic dispatch, first-class functions, an interactive loop, runtime metaprogramming. Instead of getting these for free, the program grows an ad hoc, informally specified, bug-ridden, slow version of each.
mechanism: As a system's complexity grows, it accretes configuration formats, macro and preprocessor layers, plugin systems, and eventually an ad hoc embedded interpreter or metaprogramming layer — an unplanned, informal reimplementation of the abstraction machinery a Lisp runtime already supplies.

examples.text: Large systems frequently sprout their own configuration or expression mini-languages that creep toward Turing-completeness — an ad hoc interpreter reinventing evaluation, exactly as the rule predicts. Illustrative rather than a sourced case study.
Enterprise applications commonly graft on rule engines or embedded scripting to regain the runtime flexibility a Lisp image gives natively — the metaprogramming layer arriving late and awkwardly.
Games and large C++ applications embed scripting virtual machines once static compiled code proves too rigid — the 'embedded interpreter' the rule anticipates.

variants.name: Morris's corollary
variants.text: Attributed to Robert Morris: '...including Common Lisp.' The joke is that real Lisp implementations often have a compiled low-level core, so they too contain the ad hoc half-of-Lisp. Well-attested folklore rather than a dated source.

variants.name: The inner-platform effect
variants.text: A close cousin: a system so configurable it becomes a poor reimplementation of the very platform it runs on — the same convergence toward a homegrown, worse version of what already exists.

whyItMatters: It captures a genuine pattern in the evolution of large software — the drift toward homegrown, informal versions of abstractions that mature languages already provide — while functioning as a piece of Lisp-advocacy wit. It is a memorable warning that unplanned complexity tends to reinvent, poorly, what better tools offer natively.

working.text: when a system starts growing its own config language, rule engine, or scripting layer, recognise it as reinventing evaluation — and decide whether to adopt a real language instead.
if you find yourself rebuilding garbage collection, dispatch, or metaprogramming by hand, that is the rule biting; prefer tools that supply them.

working.lead: Take it as folklore, not proof
working.text: it is an in-joke about a tendency, not a measured claim; use it to notice a pattern, not to settle a language war.

limits: It is a humorous adage and Lisp-advocacy in-joke, not an empirical claim, and it is unfalsifiable as stated — 'sufficiently complicated' and 'half of' are undefined. It is self-aware about its own naming gag (there are no rules one through nine), and Morris's corollary undercuts it by noting Lisp implementations themselves rest on lower-level cores. Cite it as folklore about programming culture, never as measured fact.
misreadings: There are no preceding nine rules — the 'tenth' is itself the joke; Greenspun has said he just wanted a memorable name. And it does not literally claim programs contain Lisp; it claims they reinvent Lisp's features informally and badly. The exact punctuation of the line varies between sources, and its date is only approximate.
origin: Coined by Philip Greenspun in the early-to-mid 1990s (commonly cited as around 1993, though he says he no longer recalls where he first wrote it). Robert Morris later appended the corollary '...including Common Lisp'.

sources.text: Greenspun's tenth rule, Wikipedia. — the canonical wording, the 'no rules 1–9' gag, and Morris's corollary.
philip.greenspun.com — Greenspun's own page, including his note that he cannot recall the original source.
